title: Why Quantum Hardware Needs Its Own Threat Model - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Guest essay by independent researcher Garrv Sipani (published under Doug Finke's byline) arguing that quantum security discourse fixates on post-quantum cryptography while the quantum computers themselves — largely classical control stacks reachable via cloud — lack any threat model. He introduces the Quantum Hardware Threat Matrix (QHTM): 5 tactics, 26 techniques with maturity tags, CC BY 4.0, filed with MITRE CWE/CAPEC.

insights.claim: Post-quantum cryptography defends classical systems against quantum computers, but almost nobody is working on defending quantum computers themselves from attack.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: An unaddressed security layer in quantum computing is a potential new product and services category.
insights.quote: Nobody in that conversation is defending the quantum computer itself.

insights.claim: A quantum computer is largely a classical machine — compiler, scheduler, calibration database, real-time control stack and classical error-correction decoder — with qubits at the end of the pipe, so it inherits ordinary software and hardware attack surfaces.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Security for quantum systems will look like classical security applied to new components; existing security vendors may extend into it.
insights.quote: The qubits are just what sits at the end of the pipe.
insights.locator: I kept running into that gap

insights.claim: Commercial quantum computing via IBM, AWS Braket, Azure Quantum, Google, IonQ and Quantinuum is a cloud business built on remote job submission, so these machines are not air-gapped and are among the most reachable computing surfaces built.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Cloud quantum providers carry real, under-discussed security exposure as enterprise usage grows.
insights.quote: it’s one of the most reachable computing surfaces we’ve ever built

insights.claim: Even an air gap does not protect a quantum machine against multi-tenant attackers who rent legitimate time on the same chip, or against supply-chain compromise via compiler and SDK dependencies.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Supply-chain and tenant-isolation controls are the relevant defenses, not network isolation.
insights.locator: And even for a device that genuinely

insights.claim: Fault-tolerant quantum machines depend on classical decoders, and feeding a decoder tampered stabilizer measurements makes it apply wrong corrections, producing logical errors indistinguishable from noise.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: As the industry moves to fault tolerance, decoder integrity becomes a security-critical component.
insights.quote: feed it tampered measurements and it will cheerfully apply the wrong correction, producing logical errors that look exactly like noise
insights.locator: So what does the surface actually look like?

insights.claim: Crosstalk between coupled qubits on multi-tenant hardware lets one tenant bias or corrupt another's computation, and dynamic circuits with mid-circuit measurement enable covert channels between registers that never share a gate.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Multi-tenant quantum cloud offerings may need hard isolation guarantees, affecting utilization economics.

insights.claim: Published research already demonstrates crosstalk side channels on multi-tenant NISQ devices, decoder-fooling attacks and silent edits to compiled circuits, but these results are scattered with no unifying framework.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: The threat is real today, not speculative, which strengthens the case for security spend.
insights.quote: Plenty of individual exploits, no framework to hang them on.

insights.claim: Quantum hardware security has gone unowned because hardware was scarce and urgent problems were physics problems, the field assumes quantum errors are random rather than malicious, and few people understand both the hardware and attacker thinking.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: A skills gap at the quantum-security intersection suggests talent scarcity and an opportunity for specialist firms.
insights.quote: There’s a quiet assumption baked in that quantum error means random error — that noise is just nature, never malice.
insights.locator: Why has nobody built that framework?

insights.claim: Mapping the quantum hardware attack surface now while it is small is far cheaper than reverse-engineering it after a first incident, a lesson the post-quantum migration already taught by starting late.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Expect adversarial attention to rise as quantum machines move to cloud and fault-tolerance roadmaps; early movers in quantum security may benefit.
insights.quote: The post-quantum migration already taught us what starting late costs.
insights.locator: The quantum industry has spent a decade

insights.claim: Just as MITRE ATT&CK gave enterprise security a shared vocabulary, quantum hardware needs a vendor-neutral, defense-agnostic catalog of attacks.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Standardized threat taxonomies tend to precede procurement requirements and compliance checklists.
insights.quote: You can’t protect what you can’t name.
insights.locator: That’s the gap a threat model fills.

insights.claim: The Quantum Hardware Threat Matrix (QHTM), authored by independent researcher Garrv Sipani, organizes quantum hardware attacks into five tactics and twenty-six techniques, each tagged as demonstrated on hardware, simulation-only, theoretical, or already mitigated.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: A ready-made framework vendors and security teams can adopt to scope quantum-specific risk.
insights.locator: That’s what I set out to build with QHTM

insights.claim: QHTM is published under CC BY 4.0 and its weaknesses and attack patterns have been filed with MITRE's CWE and CAPEC programs.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Entry into CWE/CAPEC would push quantum hardware weaknesses into mainstream security tooling.

insights.claim: QHTM's author frames it as an incomplete starting point and a map of attacks rather than defenses, noting much of the surface is genuinely early-stage.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Treat the framework as signal of direction, not as evidence of imminent exploitation at scale.
insights.quote: A threat model that cries wolf teaches people to tune it out
insights.locator: I’d rather be honest about its limits
